sections.h2: How do I reach the Portage County recorder in Ravenna?
sections.html:
The Portage County Recorder's office page prints a main line of (330) 297-3553, a fax at (330) 297-7349, and the same number for copy requests. Copy requests can also go by email to PCREC.COPIES@PORTAGECO.COM. Call before you drive a deed over to confirm counter hours.

Ravenna is the county seat, and the auditor's forms use 449 South Meridian Street as the county's address for property work. Hand-carried or mailed, a deed goes to the auditor on that street first, because the transfer there comes before recording.

Researchers should know that staff do not run the search for you. They will point you to the indexes and help you read them, and the page invites anyone studying title or family history to use the office.

sections.h2: What does the Portage County recorder keep on file?
sections.html:
The recorder's description of the office describes a permanent record of every paper that moves or burdens land here. Each filing gets a time stamp and a document number, then goes to microfilm and image storage and into the computer index.

  • Deeds, mortgages and easements.
  • Land titles and rights-of-way.
  • Federal tax liens and unemployment liens.
  • Uniform Commercial Code filings.
  • Leases of several kinds, along with veteran discharges and records of veteran burials.

Fees collected here are split between the county general fund and the state housing trust fund. The office also reminds commissioners and township trustees each year to file zoning resolutions and maps. What a seller cares about is that mortgage and lien releases appear in these same indexes, where the buyer's title examiner will look.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to record a deed in Portage County?
sections.html:
The county's fee page defers to the state schedule and gives one warning. A paper that breaks the state marginal rule picks up an added $20.00. The dollar figures below come from the statute, R.C. 317.32.

  • Pages one and two together: $34, split evenly between base and trust fund shares.
  • Every page after that: $8, again split evenly.
  • A county-set preservation surcharge, capped at $5 and paid to the general fund.
  • Certified copies: $2 per page in total.
  • Each marginal reference in a separate instrument: $4 in total.

The surcharge can be anything up to the cap, so ask the recorder for the total on your exact document. The statute counts the caption page, and any fraction of a page counts as a page.

sections.h2: What does the auditor take before a Portage County deed reaches the recorder?
sections.html:
The auditor's side comes first. According to the auditor's transfer page, the real estate department transfers deeds and similar papers ahead of recording. Its stated conveyance charge is four dollars for each $1,000 of price, plus fifty cents for every parcel moved. The DTE 100 form, Conveyance of Real Property, travels with the deed.

Use the rate Portage County prints, not a figure quoted for another county. A county board may also adopt a transfer tax on grantors of no more than 30 cents on each $100 of value, collected by the auditor ahead of recording (R.C. 322.02). Ask the auditor whether Portage has adopted one.

The same auditor's pages also offer parcel ownership histories, valuations, sales information and tax data, which are worth printing before you meet a buyer.

sections.h2: Which Portage County offices does a seller contact?
sections.html:
Three desks handle most of a sale, and each prints something different for the public.

Portage County offices a home seller usually needs, with what each published
OfficeTask in a saleWhat it publishes
RecorderRecords the deed, mortgage and releasesMain (330) 297-3553; fax (330) 297-7349; online index called Find My Deed
AuditorTransfers the deed, sets the conveyance fee$4.00 per $1,000 plus 50 cents per parcel; DTE 100 form
TreasurerBills and collects property taxTwo bills a year, about half in February and half in July

The treasurer's schedule matters because the deed does not settle unpaid tax. Get a payoff for the parcel from the treasurer, and have the title company say who bears the half now accruing.

sections.h2: Can I search Portage County land records myself?
sections.html:
Yes. The recorder's page links a "Find My Deed" search, and the county posts scanned lease books on its site, with books numbered 92 through 114 posted so far and more promised as scanning continues. The office warns that its indexes default to one page for some older volumes and pages, so documents shown as a single page may run longer. Call or email the office for correct page totals before you order copies.

Copies of all records are available on request. Bring a parcel number or the names on the deed, since staff will not search on your behalf. The auditor's property search gives the owner history and sales for a parcel, which narrows what to ask for.

The state's rule on documents also applies here: Ohio requires a conveyance to be prepared and signed under the Revised Code before it is accepted for record. The recorder's page says so in plain terms.

sections.h2: What should I have ready before I record in Portage County?
sections.html:
Bring a deed that was prepared and signed under the Ohio Revised Code, since the recorder's page says all documents to be recorded must be. Have the auditor's transfer done first, and keep the DTE 100 form with the paperwork.

  • The signed, acknowledged deed with the marginal rule observed.
  • Payment for the auditor's conveyance fee and the recorder's fees.
  • A parcel number, so staff and the online index can match the right record.

After acceptance the office stamps the time, numbers the document, films and scans it, and adds it to the index. After closing, request a copy of the recorded deed for your own file.

sections.h2: What else should a Portage County seller know about recording?
sections.html:
The county covers 504 square miles of Northeast Ohio and dates to an 1808 act of the General Assembly, per its about page. Wikipedia gives the 2020 population as 161,791 and puts rented homes at 31.1% of the occupied total.

  • Format the deed to Ohio's page and margin rules to avoid the $20 surcharge.
  • Record a mortgage satisfaction soon after payoff, so the buyer's title search is clean.
  • Visit the auditor for the transfer step before the recorder.

The recorder's office has also listed a Good Deeds Program, billed as a way to prepare now and avoid the probate court process later. Ask the office for current dates and locations if a family property may pass to heirs. The deed you record today decides how that transfer works.

A house with liens, back taxes or a stalled estate can still be sold for cash, and the buyer's closing agent handles the filings.

faqs.q: What is the Portage County recorder's phone number?
faqs.a: The main line is (330) 297-3553, and the fax is (330) 297-7349. Copy requests use the same phone number and also go by email to PCREC.COPIES@PORTAGECO.COM.

faqs.q: How much does the Portage County auditor charge to transfer a deed?
faqs.a: Four dollars per $1,000 of the price plus fifty cents a parcel, according to the auditor. The recorder's fee is separate, and the auditor's transfer happens first.

faqs.q: Is there an extra recording fee in Portage County?
faqs.a: Yes, in one case. A paper that breaks the state marginal rule picks up $20.00 on top of the usual charges, so check margins before you submit.

faqs.q: Can I look up a Portage County deed online?
faqs.a: Yes. The recorder's page links a Find My Deed search, and the auditor's real estate site shows ownership history and sales. The recorder warns that page counts on older volumes can be wrong, so confirm them by phone.

faqs.q: Does the recorder pay off my mortgage or my taxes?
faqs.a: No. The recorder files papers and nothing more. Payoffs run through your lender and the county treasurer, and a closing agent normally arranges both.
